column2: Long Christmas vacation 1936-37
Spring vacation of the fourth year: four students (two boys, two girls) go off together to Florida
Discussions on the purchase of Lake Eden (Mort Steinau's diary, April 12, 13, 30 and May 1, 1937)
Visit by Aldous Huxley (with his wife, his son, and Gerald Heard) in early May 1937; Heard talks about communities, yoga, telepathy; Huxley's notes on the United States
Knickerbocker absent for two and a half weeks without the college noticing (“his cause have practically completely folded up”)
Aldous Huxley's talk before the whole college: “limitations of the novel” (ideas and the work of art, Dickens, Homer, Fielding)
End-of-year departures: James Gore King and William Zeuch do not return; Zeuch leaves a 5,000-word critique, “The State of Black Mountain College” (“drifting into Fascism”)

Purchase of the Lake Eden property (a former resort: 667 acres, artificial lake, dining hall on piles, two lodges, a dozen cottages) for $35,000 ($2,000 down, $7,000 a year for five years) thanks to a subscription, notably from the Forbes family
Stays by the composer-cellist Dante Fiorello: he composes and plays “The Black Mountain Suite” and “The John Andrew Rice Suite”
Visits by Ted Shawn and his troupe of dancers, by Fernand Léger (translated by Lucian Marquis), and by Henry Miller (two days, with Abraham Ratner)
“Alice” enters the college (55 students in the fall) despite a negative vote (“another vampire”)
A young economist, hired at the last minute, and his wife are the target of Rice's mockery from the start of the term
Two students elope, about three months after the start of the year; the rector (Rice) more upset than anyone
Launch of the BMC Newsletter; David Bailey (a former student) director of publicity for a year
One Sunday evening, two Antioch students hitchhike to Lee Hall during Debussy's En blanc et noir for two pianos; one of them, Will Hamlin, decides to transfer to Black Mountain
Wunsch stages Irwin Shaw's Bury the Dead, with a set in sections surrounding the audience (George Hendrickson)
Schawinsky's “Danse Macabre”: total theater in the round, music by John Evarts played by the orchestra under Allan Sly, audience masked and caped
Rice and Alice's affair begins “by midwinter”; an evening of skits in which Alice, in a papier-mâché costume, parodies an opera singer; Rice says he is “shocked”
First visit by Walter Gropius (at Albers's suggestion): lecture on modern architecture (“nobody can get to essentials better than he”)
Arrival of the psychologist Erwin Straus (Germany), who buys overalls as a gesture of fellowship during the building program
John Cage (Cornish School, Seattle) writes to ask for a position; then in 1942 proposes a Center for Experimental Music; nothing comes of it
Last general meeting of the year: Wunsch sums up the Rice affair for the students (“You are in no condition to direct the College affairs now”)
Portell-Vila leaves at the end of the following year
Rice returns, a “ghostlike existence”; he writes his autobiography in a room in Lee Hall; Alice stays, the affair is over; Peggy (Loram) and David Bailey arrive
The Board elects Robert Wunsch rector in place of Rice
Nell Rice serves as hostess for her brother Aydelotte at Swarthmore, attends library school at Chapel Hill and does an apprenticeship in Asheville
Jalowetz enters the United States; through the National Coordinating Committee to Aid Refugees he learns of a vacancy at Black Mountain
BMC Newsletter no. 4 (purchase of Lake Eden)
Lake Eden run as an inn for two summers; summer courses in music and singing to raise funds
Arrival of Heinrich Jalowetz (pupil of Schoenberg, former opera conductor in Cologne and Regensburg), his wife Johanna, and his daughter Lisa, for the year 1939-40
The Cherry Orchard in rehearsal from October to May (“it would be put on when it was ready”)
BMC Newsletter no. 6: where the students come from (18 from New York, 8 from Massachusetts, 6 from Illinois; Northeast 58%)

During construction: a carload of 54 tons of coal arrives (four volunteers, three days, a steak dinner); “The Sawing Off of the Pile Posts”; a small building burns (burst pipes); three-day storm (11 inches of rain): two students swept over the spillway, one drowns
BMC Newsletter no. 7: announcement of Rice's departure (to devote himself to writing)

Stay of Aristide Mavridis (brother-in-law of the Greek ambassador Cimon Diamantopoulos, former Greek secretary general of Agriculture), come to learn English: a few weeks teaching fencing to young Eddie Dreier, then an abrupt departure

Building program begins: classes in the morning and evening, volunteer work in the afternoon at Lake Eden (drainage, insulation, foundations) for nearly three years; foreman Charles Godfrey, head carpenter Bascombe Allen; Richard Gothe organizes the crews (stones, concrete…)
A. Lawrence Kocher and his family settle at the college: he builds his plans and teaches architecture; students from Harvard (among them the Thais “Nim” and “Nik”)
Arrival of Molly Gregory (age 30): assistant to Albers, woodworking, furniture, farm; arbiter of the community
Wallen studies with Carl Rogers at Ohio State (master's degree), then again for six months in 1944; offered the chance to succeed Rogers as head of USO counseling, declines
BMC Newsletter no. 10 (progress of the construction; then no. 11 February and no. 12 March 1941)
Poster “WANTED: ZOMBIES FOR THE WORK PROGRAM”; “hot general meeting” on manual labor at a liberal arts college (Straus and the motorcycling mathematicians)
One-page report on the careers of BMC graduates
Move from Lee Hall to Lake Eden: Derek Bovington shuttles back and forth by tractor with looms, pianos, books, equipment… and all of Lee Hall's heating
Fund-raising across the country: Evarts in California (Henry Fonda, the Marches, Herman Mankiewicz; only Melvyn Douglas gives); anonymous gift of $5,000 announced by Dreier
Start of the year delayed two weeks; nearly all the students come back early to help
Arrival of Frances de Graaff (age 37, Leiden doctorate on Esenin, coming from Reed College)
First general meeting at Lake Eden: speech by Albers, back from a year of teaching at Harvard (“Life means change. Our aim is forward”)
Betty Brett's diary (November 2, 4, 25, 1941) on the students' demands
John Andrew Rice, I Came Out of the Eighteenth Century (Harper & Brothers), Harper Prize; Albers, Dreier, and Nell Rice at first refuse to read the chapter on BMC
The faculty give up their salaries beyond $10 a month; second mortgage of $18,000 (balance of the first: $11,500)
Expansion of the farm: dairy and beef herds (bull donated by Marshall Field), 500-600 chicks, vegetables, barn, dairy, cow barn; Molly Gregory runs the farm
Arrival of the musicologist Edward Lowinsky; the anthropologist Paul Radin teaches at the college
Photo 13: Nell Rice, April 1942, by Howard Dearstyne
Requests for endorsements from colleges (Antioch, Swarthmore, Reed, Frank Graham's University of North Carolina…); a quota obtained in the V-1 (Navy) and Enlisted Reserve Corps programs
New fund-raising campaign: Albers, Kocher, Mangold, and Dreier devote nearly the whole summer to it
Letters of recommendation for Frederic Cohen and Elsa Kahl: Cohen (July 20), Carleton Sprague Smith (August 7), John Martin of the New York Times (August 8), Martha Graham (August 13, 1942)
Arrival of the chemist Fritz Hansgirg and his wife (cream-colored Cadillac, Hammond organ installed in the dining hall, records: “Bach and cookies” evenings)
Arrival of Frederic (“Fritz”) Cohen, cofounder of the Ballets Jooss, Elsa Kahl, a dancer, and Eric Bentley (age 25)
The students reject the traditional “agreement” forbidding visits to the rooms of the opposite sex
Death of Richard Carpenter (lung cancer, age 31), a year after the roofing job
Mort Steinau leaves the community (financial management)
Negro History Week: talks by faculty members, Harmon Foundation film on Hampton Institute, lecture by W. A. Robinson; Wunsch invites Asheville's Black teachers
Mica mining: 250 pounds in two days; inspectors from the Colonial Mica Corporation (“good muscovite”); a miner hired
BMC Community Bulletin (summer, no. II)
The farm supplies most of the food; pork and beef sold outside; Albers has paneled and painted the dining hall and the lodge halls; gravel paths edged with galax and laurel
Arrival of Clark Foreman (New Deal, Defense Housing Authority, Southern Conference for Human Welfare)
Bentley's lectures on the war (second front); Straus's counter-series on the history of materialism; Straus invites Emilio von Hofmannsthal to warn against Russia
Hansgirg announces to the Board the creation of a company for his process of extracting magnesium from olivine and gives 20% to the college (the project comes to nothing: the pilot plant burns)

The executive committee of the Southern Conference for Human Welfare (chairman: Foreman) meets for several days at Black Mountain; two long meetings with the community on “democracy”: unanimous opinion in favor of admitting Black students

Four months of debate on admitting Black students (secret caucuses, marathon sessions); resignation of a student and of the assistant treasurer; the students vote 2 to 1 for admission from fall 1944; faculty divided (Foreman, Bentley, de Graaff, Cohen, Jalowetz, Radin for; Straus, the Alberses, Hansgirg, Kurtz, Wunsch, Gregory, Miller, Dreier, Lowinsky against)
Visit by the anthropologist Zora Hurston to Black Mountain
Students put up an exhibition of Bertrand Russell's books in the library; Straus blames de Graaff for it, and she does not speak to him for weeks
Photo 12: Eric Bentley leads a seminar, 1944
Robert Creeley, a Harvard student, spends a few days at Black Mountain with his wife Ann, briefly a student in 1944
Visit by two Black students and a Black professor from Fisk, housed in the regular dormitories after debate, without incident
Foreman, “Summary of Discussions Regarding Admission of Negro Students” (the Rosenwald Fund offers to fund Black students)
Wunsch's production of Outward Bound, mocked by the Bentleyites (“a major college disgrace”)

Surrealist costume ball “Out of This World” (Bentley: “to shock Erwin Straus”): Janey Stone, Jeanne Wacker as a “hula girl,” the Hansgirgs dressed as each other, Albers in a tweed suit with paper cones, who leaves in a fury
Dreier turns on Paul Radin (gossip, intrigue, “Communist plots”); Radin announces he will not return; the Radins leave a few days before the end of the term without notice
Summer 1944: Clark Foreman works for the CIO Committee for Political Action for Roosevelt's reelection; Eric Bentley teaches at Fisk for the summer

1944 Music Institute: nearly the entire Schoenberg circle — Rudolf Kolisch, Marcel Dick, Edward Steuermann, Ernst Krenek, Roger Sessions, Mark Brunswick; Schoenberg sends a message for the opening; Jean Charlot leaves two frescoes on the piers of the Studies Building; receipts of more than 3,000 dollars
Architectural Forum: plans of Kocher's “Jalowetz Cottage”
1944 Summer Music Institute: Kolisch Quartet, Ernst Krenek, Edward Steuermann, Yella Pessl; rehearsals of Schoenberg's Quartet op. 7 in the North Lodge hall
1944 Summer Art Institute (a week after the start of the Music Institute): Gropius, Amédée Ozenfant, José de Creeft, Jean Charlot (frescoes on the piers of the Studies Building)
José de Creeft organizes a “bullfight” to play out the anger (toreadors, picadors mixing the opponents); to no effect
Series of Board of Fellows meetings over three weeks on the de Graaff case (then Bentley); the two factions sit on opposite sides of the dining hall; de Graaff summoned twice
Final departure of the dissidents: Frances de Graaff, Eric Bentley, Frederic Cohen, Elsa Kahl, Clark Foreman, and some twenty students — a third of the college
Dreier, exhausted (“nerves were shot”), is persuaded to take a short vacation

After the split: Bentley at the Kenyon Review for a few months, then at the University of Minnesota; de Graaff with Anderson and Wacker (Greenwich Village), then with the Cohens in the house rented by the Foremans (Park Avenue); plan for a new college in an abandoned hotel ~100 miles from Washington; de Graaff at the Office of War Information, Elsa Kahl at the Army Service Groups (Russian-English dictionary)
Erwin Straus on research leave at Johns Hopkins Hospital for the year — he will never return; Kurtz also on leave
The year 1944-45 without a biologist, economist, historian, psychologist, or language teacher; Maria Hansgirg teaches French, Lowinsky Renaissance culture; students mostly new

Peggy Bennett (Cole) a student at Black Mountain in 1944-45 (she works in the office in 1947); memories: George the cook strikes the triangle at 6 and 6:30, singing from table to table (“Green Grow the Rushes, Ho!”), concerts by Jalowetz and Lowinsky, rehearsals of Bach chorales led by Jalowetz some evenings
Arrival of George Zabriskie (poet, The Mind’s Geography): “The Psychodynamics of Creativity,” “Modern Poetry,” “Verse Writing,” then French after Maria Hansgirg's heart attack; he stays 1944-45
Alfred Kazin (age 29, author of On Native Grounds) teaches a single term: courses on Melville and Blake, a small course on the Old Testament
The cow-dung episode: hostile students present a construction made of dung in Albers's Werklehre class

One January evening, after six months of preparations, Foreman announces that he is becoming secretary of the National Citizens Political Action Committee: end of the college project; Fritz Cohen tries to sell the Music Institute to other schools, then directs the Juilliard Opera Workshop; de Graaff at Wells (two years), then Bryn Mawr
Fred Schwartz (doctorate in economics from the Sorbonne, former textile manufacturer in Czechoslovakia), a few months at the college, resigns with an eight-page critique
Albers speaks in class about the election of the Student Moderator (“the preceding year”)
May 1945: the college settles on its formula — two Black students admitted to the summer institutes of music and art, then a Black teacher (or a series of visiting professors) for the fall
1945 summer institutes: two Black scholarship students and two Black guest artists, Carol Brice and Roland Hayes — fees and scholarships paid by the Julius Rosenwald Fund
